papers.title: scINTILLA: Single-Cell Integrated Inference, Labelling, and Landscape Analysis for Assessing the Quality and Hidden Diversity of Cell Annotations
papers.abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing has made it possible to build atlases of millions of cells, but the cell-type labels in these atlases are rarely checked once they are assigned. When a label covers a transcriptionally heterogeneous population, every analysis that depends on it inherits the problem, and automated label transfer in particular becomes unreliable. We present scINTILLA (Single-Cell Integrated Inference, Labelling, and Landscape Analysis), a framework that scores every label in an annotated dataset from three complementary signals: clustering confusion (neighbours that share a cluster but carry another label), label fragmentation (one label spread over several clusters) and supervised consistency (agreement, confidence and entropy of a classifier ensemble). The three signals are combined into a per-label quality score, scINTILLA-F, which can optionally be rank-fused with the Silhouette width. To test whether the score finds real annotation problems, we injected three kinds of known errors (merged labels, contaminated labels and over-split labels) into five Human Cell Atlas datasets, giving 150 perturbed annotations, and compared scINTILLA with the Silhouette baseline, kNN purity, SCCAF and ROGUE in a pre-registered analysis. The four best of the eleven methods that score every label were all scINTILLA-based. The fusion of scINTILLA-F with Silhouette ranked first (balanced AUROC 0.908; Silhouette 0.896, kNN purity 0.815, SCCAF 0.770) and improved on the Silhouette baseline in every atlas, and adding fragmentation raised the detection of merged labels in every atlas. scINTILLA and the Silhouette baseline were complementary. The Silhouette baseline was better at finding merges, whereas scINTILLA was better at finding over-split labels. Applied to the real atlases, scINTILLA flagged the ``Unknown'' and monocyte-derived macrophage labels of the lung atlas and the ``stem cell'' label of the endoderm organoid atlas. Re-analysis of these populations resolved disease-associated monocyte and macrophage states and a set of progenitor, stromal and differentiated identities with distinct tissue and protocol origins. Finally, we tested the score on merges that arise naturally, in a leukaemia atlas of 183 patients whose blast populations we had annotated. Label fragmentation revealed the diversity of the blasts hidden under a patient label: in acute myeloid leukaemia it was higher in patients whose blasts formed several populations. In each of these cases scINTILLA pointed to the labels that needed a closer look, and the interpretation remained with the expert. It is therefore advisory: it ranks labels for expert review and shows which signal flagged each one.

papers.title: CellBench: task-dependent performance and generalization limits of single-cell foundation models
papers.abstract: Single-cell foundation models (scFMs) are increasingly used for transcriptomic analysis, yet it remains unclear what biological information their embeddings preserve and when they outperform dataset-fitted methods. papers.title: Scalable cell-state-resolved TWAS identified dynamic autoimmune disease genes along functional programs
papers.abstract: Transcriptome-wide association studies (TWAS) are widely used to prioritize genes for complex diseases. TWAS typically trains models on expression quantitative disease locus (eQTL) reference data to predict gene expression from genotype, then tests for association between the predicted expression and disease. Here we propose Fast-TWiST, an accelerated and scalable version of TWiST that can analyze hundreds of thousands to millions of cells. Fast-TWiST computes donor-level summary statistics that retain all the information needed to fit the cell-level model, so numerical optimization runs over donors rather than individual cells. In simulations and real-data evaluations, Fast-TWiST was more than 10 times faster than TWiST while matching its statistical performance. papers.title: Metabolic priming recruits tumour cells across a mitochondrial vulnerability threshold and sensitizes them to chemotherapy

papers.title: Smyd1 regulates H3K4me3 to support adaptive fatty acid oxidation in the adult heart during lipid overload

papers.title: Single-molecule in situ detection and quantification of mitochondrial DNA heteroplasmy
papers.abstract: The mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) is a multi-copy genome present in most eukaryotic cells and essential for life. papers.title: Replicate libraries set the noise floor for cell-state claims in cross-sectional single-cell data: an empirical audit in drug-tolerant EGFR-mutant PC9 cells
papers.abstract: Claims that drug-tolerant cancer cells occupy stable states rest on single-cell snapshots with one sequencing library per condition, where a difference between conditions cannot be separated from a difference between libraries. No standard says how far a contrast must exceed replicate-library variation. We contribute a replicate-referenced framework: a distance ratio expressing a contrast as a multiple of the distance between replicate libraries of one condition, and a library-level permutation test giving exact p values by relabelling whole libraries. In simulations, single-library tests and a split-half reference rejected a true null in 99 to 100% of runs, and Harmony followed by a cell-level test did so in 12 to 32% with structured library effects. With four libraries per arm, the library-level test held false positives at 3 to 5% in every setting. In public osimertinib-treated PC9 data with two libraries per condition (GSE150949), halves of one library were indistinguishable, replicate libraries separated at 59 to 93% accuracy, and contrasts between times in drug and sort gates exceeded replicate distance 4.5- to 51-fold. In Drop-seq erlotinib data with one library per condition (GSE149383), two libraries of the same condition separated more readily (93.3%) than withdrawn and re-treated cells (88.5%). Cross-sectional contrasts should be reported as multiples of replicate-library distance and, with four or more libraries per arm, tested by library-level permutation. Cells moved away from the untreated profile and stayed away, but the data do not support attractor-style inference, nor do they show that tolerant states are not bistable.

papers.title: Resident liver macrophages buffer dietary and circulating cholesterol to maintain hepatocyte homeostasis
papers.abstract: Cholesterol metabolism is viewed largely through the lens of hepatocytes, leaving the roles of other liver cells unclear. These responses are heightened by elevated dietary cholesterol and occur without overt inflammation or altered liver architecture. papers.title: Spatial metabolic ecosystems shape the architecture of IDH-mutant glioma

papers.title: Rapid enhancement of antibiotic resistance and divergent remodeling of gene expression in single cells of bacteria
papers.abstract: Exposing bacterial cell populations to antibiotics often results in the emergence of descendants with enhanced resistance. Phenotypic heterogeneity and global physiological responses are thought to contribute to resistance evolution. Transcriptomic profiles of resistance-enhanced cell populations were lineage-specific, suggesting that multiple gene expression states can support enhanced resistance. Altogether, these results suggest that an interplay between initial phenotypic heterogeneity and divergent remodeling of gene expression drives the rapid acquisition of enhanced antibiotic resistance.

papers.title: Organ context dominates cell identity across a multi-organ single-cell atlas of grapevine
papers.abstract: How transcriptional programs defining cell identity are maintained or remodeled across organ contexts remains a fundamental question in plant biology, particularly in long-lived perennials. papers.title: Polymeric Biomaterials with Multiple Stratified Layers for Periodontal Ligament/Bone Regeneration: A Review.
papers.abstract: Periodontitis is a chronic pathological condition initiated by bacterial plaque accumulation and characterized by the progressive destruction of the tooth-supporting tissues, including the periodontal ligament, cementum, and alveolar bone. papers.title: Synergistic Epigenetic and Post-Transcriptional Regulation of Alveolar Bone Resorption.
papers.abstract: Alveolar bone resorption, which accompanies periodontitis, post-extraction mechanical unloading, and aging-related inflammation, is governed by interacting epigenetic and post-transcriptional mechanisms. This review integrates that evidence into a graded framework that separates mechanisms demonstrated functionally in alveolar bone or periodontal models from those supported only by correlational data or extrapolated from long-bone, calvarial, and osteoporosis models, and assigns each mechanism to the cell types in which it has been demonstrated. Because the effects of individual regulators (for example, DNMTs, HDACs, and m6A writers) depend on cell type, differentiation stage, dose, and timing, conflicting reports are examined explicitly. We further dissect the bidirectional crosstalk between epigenetic modifiers and ncRNAs, distinguishing experimentally verified links from hypothetical ones, and critically assess emerging therapeutic strategies-small-molecule epigenetic inhibitors, oligonucleotide therapeutics, and biomaterial-assisted delivery-together with their safety and delivery barriers. By formalizing an evidence-graded conceptual framework, this review provides a basis for mechanism-based strategies against alveolar bone resorption.

papers.title: Application of Ultrasound in Cutaneous Melanoma Care: A Narrative Review.
papers.abstract: Cutaneous melanoma is an aggressive skin tumour that accounts for significant mortality. Diagnosis relies on clinical examination and histopathological work-up after surgical removal. Tumour thickness (Breslow depth), determined by the pathologist, is crucial for staging and treatment. Cross-sectional imaging is mainly used to detect metastases, while sonography serves to identify pathologic lymph nodes and guide interventions. However, advances in ultrasound technology provide promising non-invasive evaluation of primary tumours that complements conventional methods. Our aim is to briefly review the currently available ultrasound-based techniques for diagnosing and managing cutaneous melanoma. High-frequency ultrasound can precisely evaluate tumour depth, competing with histopathological measurement. Doppler techniques and elastography, by mapping vascularity and tissue stiffness, provide additional clues to differentiate benign and malignant lesions. Contrast-enhanced ultrasound is not only a valuable tool for characterising the primary tumour and searching for relapse/metastasis, but it is also applied in targeted therapies. New wave ultrasound-based treatment options like sonoporation, sonodynamic therapy, and high-intensity focused ultrasound show promising preclinical results. Adopting artificial intelligence into melanoma care may reduce variability and increase diagnostic and therapeutic accuracy, though clinical validation remains limited.

papers.title: Regenerative Advances in Burn Care: iPSC-Derived MSCs as a Next-Generation Therapy for Burn Wound Healing.
papers.abstract: Severe burn injuries represent a major challenge to regenerative medicine since the damaged tissue must be repaired rapidly to avoid fatal complications; however, successful healing necessitates far more than closing the wounds. Although conventional skin grafting and biomaterial substitutes have improved wound coverage and survival, they often fall short of restoring the complex structure and function of native skin. Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) introduced a biologically active approach to combat this problem. However, their clinical translation has been hindered by classical MSC challenges, including limited scalability, donor-based variability, and age-associated functional decline. The emergence of iPSC-derived mesenchymal stem cells (iMSCs) as potent, scalable, and immunologically compatible stem cells offers an opportunity to address these challenges. In this review, we outline the evolution of stem cell-based approaches to burn wound healing, from conventional somatic MSCs to iMSCs. We evaluate evidence supporting iMSCs as a potentially superior regenerative platform. Furthermore, we discuss the emerging cell-free alternatives that retain regenerative signalling while addressing the limitations of cell-based therapies. Collectively, this review provides evidence that iMSCs not only represent an advance in MSC therapies but also a vanguard for a new generation of standardized, scalable, and biologically superior therapies for burn injuries.

papers.title: Proteomic Signatures of Vulnerability Across Late-Life Depression, Frailty, and Neurodegeneration.
papers.abstract: Late-life depression (LLD) is increasingly recognized as a complex multisystem disorder associated with accelerated biological aging, impaired physiological resilience, frailty, and an increased risk of cognitive decline and dementia. Although growing evidence supports the close relationship between depression, frailty, and neurodegeneration, the molecular mechanisms underlying this continuum remain incompletely understood. In particular, conventional clinical and imaging biomarkers capture established disease but provide limited insight into the systemic biological processes that precede neurodegeneration. Proteomics has emerged as a powerful systems biology approach capable of characterizing the dynamic molecular networks involved in aging, neuropsychiatric disorders, and neurodegenerative diseases. Recent advances in high-throughput mass spectrometry have identified alterations in proteins associated with chronic inflammation, complement activation, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, lipid metabolism, synaptic integrity, neurotrophic signaling, and cellular senescence across LLD, frailty, cognitive impairment, and Alzheimer's disease (AD). These convergent proteomic signatures suggest that these conditions may share common biological pathways consistent with progressive loss of physiological resilience rather than independent pathological entities. In this review, we examine the current evidence supporting shared proteomic mechanisms linking LLD, frailty, cognitive frailty (CF), and neurodegeneration. We discuss the potential integration of large-scale proteomic profiling with established AD biomarkers within the AT(N) framework to improve biological characterization, early risk stratification, and prediction of cognitive decline. Particular emphasis is placed on CF as a transitional and potentially modifiable phenotype in which systemic molecular dysregulation precedes overt neurodegeneration. By integrating evidence from geroscience, neuropsychiatry, and proteomics, we propose that proteomic profiling can redefine LLD and frailty as manifestations of a common biological vulnerability continuum. This systems-level perspective may facilitate the identification of individuals at high risk for dementia, support the development of multimodal biomarker panels, and advance precision neuropsychiatry through earlier diagnosis and personalized preventive interventions.

papers.title: Primary Stability of an Expandable Versus a Conventional Short Implant in Low-Density Bone: A Density-Stratified Ex Vivo Comparison.
papers.abstract: Background: Rehabilitation of atrophic posterior jaws is often challenging due to anatomical limitations, frequently requiring bone augmentation procedures or the use of short implants. Expandable short implants are characterized by an expansion mechanism whose potential contribution to primary stability remains to be fully established. This ex vivo study compared the primary stability of expandable and conventional short implants in porcine rib bone of low and intermediate CBCT-defined density (corresponding approximately to Misch D4 and D3). Methods: A total of 68 implants were placed in 17 fresh porcine ribs, using a randomized complete block design: 34 expandable short implants (ESI; Pyramidion, Ø4.1 × 5 mm) and 34 conventional short implants (CSI; Osstem TS III, Ø4 × 7 mm), equally distributed between two CBCT-defined density strata (D3 and D4, operationally defined). Peak insertion torque (PIT), resonance frequency analysis (ISQ; before and after apical expansion for the ESI group), peak removal torque (PRT), and expansion torque (ESI group only) were recorded. Data were analyzed using a two-way ANOVA (implant group × bone density) with a Bonferroni-corrected significance threshold (α = 0.025) for the two primary outcomes, ISQ and PRT. Results: PIT did not differ significantly between groups in D3 bone, while CSI showed higher PIT in D4 bone (p = 0.0005). ISQ increased significantly following apical expansion in the ESI group (mean + 4.91, 95% CI 3.60 to 6.22; p = 0.0004), more markedly in D4 than D3 bone; final ISQ did not differ significantly between groups at either bone density. PRT was higher in the ESI group in both density strata (p = 0.0004 in D3 and p = 0.0003 in D4), with no significant implant group × bone density interaction. Incomplete apical expansion occurred in 3 of 34 ESI implants, all in D3 bone. Conclusions: In this ex vivo model, no statistically significant difference in final ISQ was detected between the expandable and conventional short implants, and removal torque was higher for the expandable implant across both bone densities; equivalence was not tested. These findings refer to the initial mechanical behaviour under the tested ex vivo conditions, without implying superiority over conventional implant designs; further studies are warranted.

papers.title: Clinical Outcomes at 2 Years and Early Radiographic Changes Following Transcrestal Sinus Floor Elevation in Sites with Residual Bone Height Below or Above 4 mm: A Retrospective Comparative Cohort Study.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Maxillary sinus floor elevation is a well-established procedure for enabling implant placement in the posterior maxilla when residual bone height is insufficient. Minimally invasive transcrestal techniques, including the use of the Crestal Approach Sinus (CAS) kit, have been developed to reduce surgical morbidity while maintaining predictable clinical outcomes. The aim of this retrospective comparative study was to evaluate the clinical and radiographic outcomes of transcrestal sinus floor elevation performed using the CAS kit in patients presenting with residual bone height below or above 4 mm. Methods: Forty-five partially edentulous patients who received single implant-supported rehabilitations in the posterior maxilla between September 2021 and October 2024 were included. Patients were allocated to a test group (residual bone height Results: No implant or prosthetic failures and no biological or technical complications were recorded, resulting in 100% implant and prosthetic survival rates. Residual bone height was significantly lower in the test group (2.8 ± 0.8 mm) than in the control group (5.3 ± 1.0 mm) (p p p = 0.742) and at prosthetic delivery (12.6 ± 1.6 mm vs. 12.9 ± 1.6 mm; p = 0.556). Bone height above the implant apex was also similar between the groups at both time points. A modest but statistically significant reduction in augmented bone height was observed during healing in both groups. Conclusions: Within the limitations of this retrospective study, transcrestal sinus floor elevation using the hydraulic CAS-kit technique showed favorable clinical and radiographic outcomes in both groups, including sites with residual bone height below 4 mm. These preliminary findings suggest that the crestal approach may represent a treatment option in carefully selected patients with limited residual bone height. However, larger prospective controlled studies with standardized radiographic assessments and longer follow-up periods are needed to confirm these findings.

papers.title: Time-stratified supragingival plaque microbiome profiles after alveolar bone grafting.
papers.abstract: BackgroundAlveolar bone grafting (ABG) restores continuity of the cleft alveolus, but supragingival plaque microbiota at different intervals after grafting remain poorly characterized. We examined plaque microbial profiles in participants with ungrafted alveolar clefts, participants sampled at three intervals after ABG, and healthy controls.MethodsThis cross-sectional secondary analysis included 90 participants: 33 in the ungrafted alveolar cleft plaque group (AC-P), 14 in the early post-ABG plaque group (5 years; LABG-P), and 23 healthy controls (HC-P). Pooled supragingival plaque was analyzed by 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Alpha diversity, Bray-Curtis and weighted UniFrac community structure, a comparison-specific microbial dysbiosis index (MDI), and genus-level differences were evaluated. Exploratory Bray-Curtis comparisons were performed among the three post-ABG groups.ResultsSobs and Chao1 differed among the five groups (false discovery rate [FDR]-adjusted P = 0.0171 and 0.0157), whereas Shannon and Simpson did not. Bray-Curtis and weighted UniFrac PERMANOVA were significant (R2 = 0.0686, P = 0.010; R2 = 0.0960, P = 0.004), with the Bray-Curtis group association remaining significant after age adjustment (P = 0.006). Among the 34 post-ABG participants, neither the unadjusted nor age-adjusted three-group Bray-Curtis comparison was significant (P = 0.2790 and 0.2394), and no pairwise comparison was significant after Holm correction. After full-process permutation and FDR correction, MDI differences were significant for AC-P, EABG-P, and LABG-P versus HC-P, but not for MABG-P. Twenty-one genera remained FDR-significant in AC-P versus HC-P, compared with one in EABG-P and none in MABG-P or LABG-P.ConclusionsSupragingival plaque microbial richness and community structure differed among the five groups, while FDR-supported genus-level differences were concentrated in the ungrafted alveolar cleft group. This interval-stratified analysis extends the characterization of plaque microbial communities to patients sampled several years after ABG.

papers.title: Within-Device Exposure-Setting and Voxel-Size Changes in CBCT Alveolar Bone Measurement for Implant Planning: A Systematic Review.
papers.abstract: BackgroundThis review examined whether within-device exposure-setting or nominal voxel-size changes in cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) affect linear alveolar bone measurements for implant planning, separating accuracy from agreement.MethodsDatabase-specific search strategies and retrieval counts are reported for PubMed/MEDLINE, Ovid Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science Core Collection. Study selection is presented in the updated PRISMA flow diagram. The reported International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) identifier is CRD420261361509. Studies were grouped by outcome, protocol contrast, and experimental model. The Quality Assessment Tool for In Vitro Studies (QUIN) appraisal was performed by one reviewer. A revision-stage source and analysis-unit audit led to withdrawal of the planned inverse-variance meta-analyses and their ±0.5 mm equivalence claims; structured study-level synthesis was used instead.ResultsEight studies addressed linear measurements; two additional reports were retained only as methodological context. Seven linear-measurement studies compared protocols within a device, and one compared different devices. All were experimental. In one five-skull study, mean absolute errors were 0.50, 0.46, and 0.51 mm at 40, 20, and 7 s, respectively. A cadaver study reported mean absolute errors of approximately 1.10-1.20 mm. Small mean between-protocol differences sometimes coexisted with impaired anatomical visibility. Repeated observations were not equivalent to independent specimens, and several required sampling variances could not be reconstructed.ConclusionsSelected within-device protocol changes may preserve average measurements under controlled experimental conditions. The evidence does not establish statistical equivalence, interchangeability of protocol classes, or clinical safety near critical anatomy. Validation in living patients is needed before broad implementation.

papers.title: Allogenic Tooth Transplantation Using 3D-Printed Donor-Tooth Replicas: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: Background: Allogenic tooth transplantation has been reported for several decades, but clinical evidence remains limited, particularly regarding contemporary digital workflows, immunological characterization, and long-term outcomes. Cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT), computer-aided design/computer-aided manufacturing (CAD/CAM), and three-dimensional (3D) printing may facilitate preoperative planning and recipient-site preparation while minimizing manipulation of donor teeth. Case Report: A 48-year-old woman underwent allogenic transplantation of two mature maxillary first premolars donated by her 17-year-old son. The corresponding recipient teeth (14 and 24) had been absent for more than 10 years following unsuccessful endodontic treatment. CBCT-based planning and 3D-printed donor-tooth replicas were used to prepare the recipient sites before donor extraction. Owing to anatomical differences in root morphology and recipient-site dimensions, the teeth were transplanted contralaterally (donor 14 to recipient 24 and donor 24 to recipient 14). The extra-alveolar time was approximately 20 s for each tooth. Clinical, periodontal, radiographic, and immunogenetic assessments were performed during postoperative follow-up. Results: At 12 months, both transplanted teeth remained functional without clinically apparent complications. Periodontal probing depths remained unchanged between the 3- and 12-month examinations (tooth 14: 3.5 mm mesially and 4.0 mm distally; tooth 24: 3.0 mm mesially and 3.5 mm distally), with no bleeding on probing and mobility grade 0. No radiographically apparent pathological root resorption or ankylosis was identified. Post-transplant immunogenetic testing demonstrated donor-specific anti-HLA class I and II reactivity. Anti-MICA antibodies were not detected. In the absence of pre-transplant serum, the detected donor-specific antibodies could not be classified as pre-existing or de novo. Conclusions: CBCT-based planning and 3D-printed donor-tooth replicas facilitated the technically feasible transplantation of two mature allogenic premolars, with favorable short-term clinical findings at 12 months. Despite this clinical stability, donor-directed anti-HLA reactivity was detected after transplantation. These findings neither establish immunological tolerance nor demonstrate that the observed alloimmune reactivity was induced by transplantation. Longer follow-up and prospective immunological monitoring are required to evaluate graft survival and the clinical significance of donor-specific antibodies.

papers.title: CBCT-Based Volumetric Assessment of Tooth Roots in the Context of Alveolar Ridge Preservation.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Alveolar ridge preservation (ARP) is commonly performed following tooth extraction to minimize post-extraction dimensional changes. However, limited information is available regarding root-volume variations among different tooth types. This study aimed to assess the root volumes of maxillary and mandibular teeth using cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) and to compare the measured root volumes with commonly available graft-material package volumes in the context of ARP. Methods: CBCT scans from 53 patients meeting the eligibility criteria were retrospectively evaluated. Fourteen teeth per scan were assessed using a split-mouth approach, resulting in a total of 742 teeth. Root boundaries were identified by two trained and calibrated dentists, and root volumes were calculated using OsiriX MD v13.0.3 software. Statistical comparisons were performed using paired and independent t-tests. Results: Root volumes varied according to tooth type and arch. The maxillary first molar demonstrated the highest mean root volume (0.55 ± 0.10 cm3), whereas the mandibular central incisor demonstrated the lowest (0.11 ± 0.02 cm3). Maxillary teeth showed significantly greater root volumes than their mandibular counterparts. Gender-related differences were limited to the maxillary second premolar and mandibular second molar and were considered of limited clinical relevance. For illustrative comparison, the measured root volumes were considered in relation to commonly available graft-material package volumes, including 0.25 and 0.50 cc; these comparisons do not represent clinically validated graft requirements. Conclusions: This study provides CBCT-derived reference root-volume values for different tooth types and demonstrates variations according to tooth type and arch. Comparison of these measurements with commonly available graft-material package volumes may provide a descriptive volumetric reference in the context of ARP. However, root volume does not directly represent post-extraction socket volume or the quantity of graft material required clinically. Therefore, these comparisons should not be interpreted as recommendations for graft quantity, and prospective clinical studies comparing root volume with actual socket volume and graft utilization are required before clinical application.

Overall, 277 teeth were extracted in the discontinuation group and 195 in the continuation group. We compared the incidence of AO between the two groups and performed logistic regression analysis to identify factors associated with AO.ResultsAO occurred in 6/277 teeth (2.2%) in the discontinuation group and 18/195 teeth (9.2%) in the continuation group. Mandibular extraction was also associated with higher odds of AO. OC/LEP type was not significantly associated with AO. AO incidence in the 4-week discontinuation group was 2.3%, which was significantly lower than that in the continuation group (p = 0.007). papers.title: Regenerative Endodontic Revitalization of a Traumatized Immature Permanent Maxillary Central Incisor.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Regenerative endodontic procedures have fundamentally changed the management of immature permanent teeth with pulpal necrosis by shifting the therapeutic focus from artificial apical barrier formation to biologically driven tissue regeneration. Unlike conventional apexification, revitalization aims to restore a functional intracanal environment that supports continued root maturation, dentinal wall thickening and apical closure. The present study describes the clinical application and long-term outcome of regenerative endodontic revitalization in a traumatically injured immature permanent maxillary central incisor. Methods: An 11-year-old patient presented with a traumatized immature permanent maxillary central incisor exhibiting pulpal necrosis and an open apex. Following clinical and radiographic assessment, a regenerative endodontic protocol was performed. Canal disinfection was achieved using 1.5% sodium hypochlorite irrigation and calcium hydroxide as the intracanal medicament. At the subsequent appointment, bleeding was intentionally induced beyond the apical foramen to establish an autologous blood clot scaffold. The canal was sealed coronally with a bioceramic material and restored with a definitive composite restoration. Clinical and radiographic follow-up, including cone-beam computed tomography, was performed over a three-year period. Results: Throughout the observation period, the treated tooth remained asymptomatic and functional, with no clinical or radiographic evidence of persistent apical pathology. Serial radiographs and CBCT examinations demonstrated progressive root maturation, increased dentinal wall thickness, continued root elongation and complete apical closure. Functional integrity and esthetic appearance were maintained during the entire follow-up period. Conclusions: This case demonstrates that regenerative endodontic treatment can result in favorable clinical and radiographic outcomes for immature permanent teeth with pulpal necrosis following traumatic injury. When performed according to contemporary regenerative protocols, the procedure can facilitate continued root development and improve the long-term structural integrity of the tooth. Revascularization should be considered a valuable treatment option in appropriately selected immature permanent teeth, while long-term follow-up remains essential to evaluate healing and treatment stability.

papers.title: Osteoimmunomodulatory and Mechanobiology-Guided Biomaterials for Craniofacial and Alveolar Bone Regeneration.
papers.abstract: Craniofacial and alveolar bone regeneration remains a major challenge due to the complex anatomical, mechanical and inflammatory environment of the oral cavity. Traditional biomaterials, largely designed for osteoconduction or osteoinduction, often fail to achieve predictable outcomes in vivo, highlighting the need for strategies that actively regulate the regenerative microenvironment. Recent advances in osteoimmunology and mechanobiology have highlighted the importance of immune responses and mechanical cues in bone regeneration. Redox processes provide an additional perspective for examining how the local microenvironment may modify these responses. In this review, we focus on osteoimmunomodulatory and mechanobiology-guided biomaterial design, discussing redox regulation where it informs immune-mechanical interactions and material function. We highlight key design strategies, including surface engineering, scaffold architecture, bioactive ion release, and immunoregulatory factor delivery, together with selected responsive biomaterials and extracellular vesicle-based delivery systems. Finally, we address the major challenges limiting clinical translation and discuss how material functions may be coordinated with the changing immune and mechanical requirements of repair, while identifying gaps between proposed mechanisms and available evidence.

papers.title: Alloplastic total temporomandibular joint replacement for progressive and idiopathic condylar resorption: a scoping review of clinical outcomes, stability, and complications.
papers.abstract: Evidence regarding the efficacy, stability, and clinical outcomes of alloplastic total temporomandibular joint replacement (TMJR) for managing progressive condylar resorption (PCR) and idiopathic condylar resorption (ICR) was reviewed. A PRISMA‑ScR‑compliant search was conducted across seven electronic databases from inception to February 2026; 1324 records were screened and 37 studies included, encompassing TMJR cohorts and contextual comparator series; within these, approximately 480 patients were treated with alloplastic TMJR for PCR/ICR, alongside smaller cohorts managed with orthognathic surgery or autogenous reconstruction. While traditional orthognathic surgery in PCR/ICR populations is associated with high skeletal relapse rates (often 31-100%), alloplastic TMJR provides superior stability, with cephalometric changes generally within 0-3% of immediate postoperative values in long‑term series. Postoperative maximum incisal opening improves from severely restricted ranges (8-25 mm) to functional ranges (30-42 mm; mean gain approximately 17-18 mm). Pain scores typically decrease by approximately 75-87%, with most cohorts reporting complete or near‑complete pain relief in the majority of patients. Diagnostic innovations such as Hounsfield Unit (HU) analysis, with a characteristic sclerotic peak around 1350-1500 HU, offer objective differentiation between ICR and osteoarthritis. Complication rates for TMJR, including heterotopic ossification and infection, are generally low in contemporary series, particularly when adjunctive autologous fat grafting and patient‑specific custom prostheses are used. Alloplastic TMJR is an acceptable and safe option for end‑stage PCR/ICR in appropriately selected patients. Success is likely optimized by combining prosthetic reconstruction with adjunctive autologous fat grafting and comprehensive pain management, including assessment for central sensitization.

papers.title: Mapping anatomical factors associated with unfavorable fractures during sagittal split osteotomy: a scoping review of computed tomography-based evidence.
papers.abstract: Unfavorable fractures during sagittal split osteotomy (SSO) represent a clinically relevant complication that may compromise surgical stability and postoperative outcomes. This scoping review aimed to map the computed tomography (CT)/cone-beam-CT-assessed mandibular anatomical factors reported in relation to unfavorable fractures during SSO and to identify gaps in the current evidence. A comprehensive search was conducted in multiple databases from inception to February 2026, including analytical and descriptive studies evaluating anatomical factors. Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, data were charted regarding study characteristics, demographic data, osteotomy technique, incidence and classification of unfavorable fractures, imaging modality, anatomical factors and measurement sites, and reported associations between anatomical factors and unfavorable patterns. Sixteen studies comprising 2576 patients were analyzed, with reported unfavorable fracture incidence ranging from 1.28% to 29.2% per patient and from 0.6% to 20.65% per surgical side. Reduced buccolingual ramus thickness at the lingula level and a narrow distance between the mandibular canal and the buccal cortex were frequently reported as factors associated with unfavorable fractures. Other parameters, such as trabecular bone characteristics and regional density variations, appeared to influence fracture propagation, whereas age, sex, and third molars showed inconsistent clinical relevance. Critical evidence gaps identified include the lack of standardized definitions, inconsistent use of classification systems, and variation in anatomical landmarks. Mandibular anatomy appears to influence fracture behavior through localized structural constraints. However, due to significant methodological heterogeneity across the literature, these features should be interpreted as reported associations rather than definitive independent predictors.

papers.title: Beyond volumetrics: color-coded distance mapping reveals spatial remodeling of jaw cysts after decompression.
papers.abstract: Decompression is widely used as a first-stage treatment for large jaw cysts because it reduces lesion size and promotes bone regeneration before definitive enucleation. Conventional volumetric assessment quantifies overall shrinkage but does not describe the spatial pattern of cyst remodeling. This retrospective cohort study evaluated whether semi-automated three-dimensional segmentation combined with color-coded distance mapping provides spatial information beyond volumetric assessment after decompression. Patients with jaw cysts treated by decompression who had pre-decompression and follow-up postoperative cone-beam computed tomography scans obtained at least 6 months apart were included. Outcomes included percentage and absolute volume reduction, surface area reduction, shrinkage speed, and detailed surface deviation metrics derived from color-coded distance mapping. The study included 42 patients with a mean age of 47 ± 11 years and a mean decompression duration of 7.52 ± 1.99 months. Mean lesion volume decreased from 3.99 to 1.39 cm3, corresponding to an absolute reduction of 2.60 cm3 and a mean percentage reduction of 63.05% (P 2, corresponding to an absolute reduction of 7.57 cm2 and a mean percentage reduction of 41.3% (P < 0.001). Color-coded distance mapping demonstrated inward surface contraction in all cases and provided remodeling patterns not captured by volumetric analysis alone, with a mean surface deviation of 1.15 ± 0.37 mm and root mean square deviation of 1.40 ± 0.46 mm. Color-coded distance mapping complements volumetric assessment by revealing the spatial pattern of jaw cyst remodeling after decompression and may improve radiographic evaluation before definitive surgery.

papers.title: Interface-specific functional coatings for soft-tissue integration of craniofacial implants: oral mucosa, percutaneous skin, and muscle.
papers.abstract: Soft tissue integration (STI) is essential for limiting inflammation, maintaining craniofacial implant stability, and supporting long-term function. This narrative review evaluates functional coatings at three distinct interfaces: oral mucosa around dental abutments, craniofacial muscle and enthesis around temporomandibular joint (TMJ) prostheses, and skin around percutaneous implants. We distinguish direct integrative effects from infection control and immunomodulation, and appraise evidence from cellular responses through tissue-level outcomes. Oral mucosa requires a rapid epithelial and connective-tissue seal under continuous plaque exposure; percutaneous skin requires suppression of epithelial downgrowth and pocket formation across a chronically exposed breach; and muscle-facing temporomandibular joint components require enthesis-like anchorage and load transfer under repetitive motion. The evidence is strongest for cell-level responses and selected preclinical mucosal or skin outcomes, whereas coating-mediated TMJ muscle attachment remains at proof-of-concept stage in non-TMJ models. Negative animal findings further show that favorable cell behavior or added antibacterial activity does not necessarily produce a durable tissue seal. Interface-specific coatings should therefore be designed around a primary tissue-level endpoint, with antimicrobial and immunomodulatory functions treated as supportive and dose-limited.

papers.title: Ipsilateral tooth-registered surgical guides for minimally invasive Le Fort I osteotomy.
papers.abstract: Patient-specific surgical guides and virtual surgical planning have improved the accuracy of orthognathic surgery; however, most available systems require extensive surgical exposure that conflicts with minimally invasive Le Fort I osteotomy. This technical note describes a computer-aided design/computer-aided manufacturing guide system incorporating an ipsilateral tooth-registration stop engaging the maxillary incisors and canine, combined with independent bilateral guide insertion. Guides were designed in 3-matic software (Materialise, Leuven, Belgium) following ProPlan CMF virtual surgical planning, prototyped in biocompatible resin, and definitively manufactured in cobalt-chromium alloy by laser powder-bed fusion. The design integrates osteotomy trajectory definition, fixation-hole predrilling, and three-dimensional plate registration within a single device. Independent bilateral insertion reduces individual guide dimensions, facilitating placement through limited surgical access. Dental registration is intended to support reproducible guide seating while reducing reliance on extensive skeletal exposure. Rather than a new concept, the system represents a technical refinement of previously described occlusal-supported and bilaterally separated minimally invasive guide designs, integrating dental support, bilateral modularity, and multifunctional guidance-including three-dimensional plate registration-within a single digital workflow; its reproducibility and accuracy remain to be evaluated in future studies.

papers.title: Management Strategies for Trigeminal Neuralgia: A Systematic Review and Pooled Analysis.
papers.abstract: PurposeTrigeminal neuralgia (TN) is one of the most debilitating neuropathic facial pain disorders. Although carbamazepine remains the first-line pharmacologic therapy, many patients become refractory or intolerant to long-term medication, necessitating surgical intervention. Multiple operative techniques are available; however, comparative durability and complication profiles remain heterogeneous. This systematic review aimed to evaluate the effectiveness, recurrence rates, and safety of pharmacologic and surgical management strategies for TN.MethodsA systematic review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Electronic databases including PubMed, MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched for studies evaluating medical and surgical treatments of TN. Randomized controlled trials, prospective and retrospective cohort studies, and systematic reviews reporting measurable pain outcomes were included. Primary outcomes were immediate pain relief and long-term pain freedom (≥3 y). Secondary outcomes included recurrence rates, sensory complications, and quality-of-life measures.ResultsTwenty-nine studies met inclusion criteria. Carbamazepine demonstrated effective initial pain control but limited long-term durability due to adverse effects and recurrence. Microvascular decompression (MVD) provided the highest immediate relief (94%) and durable long-term pain freedom (72%). Percutaneous procedures (radiofrequency thermocoagulation, balloon compression, glycerol rhizotomy) showed high initial relief (85%-91%) but increased recurrence and sensory morbidity. Stereotactic radiosurgery demonstrated moderate long-term control with low perioperative morbidity but delayed onset of action. Outcomes in multiple sclerosis-associated TN were inferior compared with classic TN.ConclusionsMicrovascular decompression remains the gold standard surgical intervention for medically refractory classic TN in appropriate candidates. Percutaneous and radiosurgical techniques offer effective alternatives for elderly or medically compromised patients. Standardized outcome reporting and high-quality comparative trials are required to refine treatment algorithms.

papers.title: Use of a Transconjunctival Flap for Ocular Protection in the Management of Orbital Floor and Medial Wall Fractures.
papers.abstract: IntroductionOrbital floor and medial wall fractures are commonly managed through transconjunctival approaches due to their favorable aesthetic outcomes and direct surgical access. A conjunctival flap was elevated and temporarily sutured to the upper eyelid during surgery to protect the globe and cornea while maintaining adequate surgical exposure. Clinical records, intraoperative findings, and postoperative outcomes were reviewed.ResultsEleven patients with isolated orbital floor fractures, isolated medial wall fractures, or combined defects were included. Adequate surgical exposure was achieved in all cases while maintaining continuous ocular protection throughout the procedure. Orbital reconstruction was performed using titanium mesh when required. By integrating ocular protection into the surgical approach itself, the technique preserves adequate surgical exposure without requiring additional protective devices and may represent a safe and practical adjunct during transconjunctival orbital surgery.

papers.abstract: ObjectiveTo systematically evaluate clinical evidence on patient-specific implants (PSIs) in mandibular and temporomandibular surgery, stratified by indication, biomaterials, outcomes, and complications.Materials and methodsPubMed and Scopus were searched up to January 2026 (PROSPERO: CRD42024580864). papers.title: Primary sclerosing cholangitis: epidemiology, risk factors, pathophysiology, clinical features, diagnosis, and management.
papers.abstract: Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) is a rare cholangiopathy characterized by multifocal inflammation and fibrostenotic remodeling of the bile ducts, cholestasis, and increased risks of cholangiocarcinoma and colorectal cancer. No pharmacological therapy has yet improved transplant-free survival. Clinical care therefore depends on accurate phenotyping, surveillance, treatment of biliary and intestinal complications, and timely liver transplantation. Population-based and clinical studies define the epidemiology, risk factors, presentation, diagnosis, and management of PSC. Studies of human biospecimens, including microbiome and metabolomic analyses, describe biological changes associated with the disease, whereas organoid and animal models are used to investigate potential mechanisms. The available evidence links genetic susceptibility and PSC-associated inflammatory bowel disease to cholangiocyte injury, immune activation, disturbed bile acid homeostasis, and microbial alterations. At the bile duct interface, cholangiocyte senescence and barrier dysfunction may interact with microbial exposure and immune-cell recruitment to promote periductal fibrosis. PSC is therefore more plausibly viewed as a multicellular process than as the consequence of a single microbial, immune, or bile acid pathway. Whether dysbiosis and altered bile acid profiles contribute to disease development or instead reflect established PSC remains unresolved. Concomitant inflammatory bowel disease, medication use, biliary obstruction, and previous biliary interventions further complicate causal inference. Longitudinal human studies may distinguish early drivers from secondary changes. Mechanistic findings should ultimately improve patient phenotyping, surveillance, endoscopic management, and selection for targeted trials. Such trials will require biologically informed designs and endpoints that capture durable clinical benefit.

Follow-up CBCT revealed a mixed osteolytic-osteosclerotic process at the same site, with mandibular canal involvement, and sequestrum formation. Surgical excision and histopathologic examination confirmed MRONJ. CONCLUSIONS This case highlights the value of longitudinal CBCT in documenting the radiographic evolution of MRONJ at the site of a previously identified lesion provisionally diagnosed as a DBI. However, the observed temporal and spatial association does not establish a causal relationship between the baseline lesion and subsequent development of MRONJ.

papers.abstract: The spinal cord is the primary relay center between the periphery and the brain, playing a critical role in sensory, motor and autonomic function. papers.title: Spatial causal discovery reveals novel mechanisms of cellular senescence in human liver
papers.abstract: The complex network of mechanisms that surround cellular senescence, such as its precise causes and effects, are not entirely understood at present. Senescent cells are present in both healthy and unhealthy tissue, but their abundance is positively correlated with disease and age. A better understanding of senescence could lead to healthier aging, improved recovery from chemotherapy, or increased lifespan. We show that Visium data from human liver tissue satisfies the causal Markov condition. 3. papers.title: A Registration-Free and Slope-aware Framework for CBCT-based Dental Implant Planning.
papers.abstract: Precise planning of dental implant placement is crucial for oral rehabilitation, yet current AI-based automated methods heavily rely on accurately annotated data. Prevailing approaches obtain training labels by registering pre- and post-implantation CBCT scans, which suffers from low registration accuracy and limited paired data availability. Furthermore, implant-position prediction can benefit from explicit supervision of implant orientation to guide anatomical feature learning. To address these issues, this paper proposes RegFreeNet, a novel registration-free framework. Motivated by the clinical insight that implant positioning is largely determined by the morphology of neighboring teeth, RegFreeNet learns directly from unpaired post-implantation CBCT scans with masked implant regions, thereby eliminating the dependence on registration algorithm. However, removing implant structures introduces new challenges. The occlusion of the mandibular nerve canal within the masked region raises safety concerns regarding anatomical localization. To tackle this, we design a Neighboring Distance Perception (NDP) module, which combines multi-scale convolutions with graph-based spatial context aggregation to recover anatomical context for implant position prediction . We further introduce a slope prediction branch that shares encoder features with the implant position prediction branch. Auxiliary supervision from reference implant slopes guides shared feature learning through joint optimization of implant position and slope prediction. To validate our method, we contribute ImplantFairy, the first large-scale public dataset for dental implant planning, comprising 1,622 implant-specific CBCT samples. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RegFreeNet achieves state-of-the-art performance. Dataset access: https://github. com/sanjinYoung/ImplantFairy.

papers.abstract: The paper presents an effective fault-element detection method for conformal array antennas based on a spherical spatial deconvolution. papers.title: Fibrotic Scars and the Potential Therapeutics After Spinal Cord Injury.
papers.abstract: Spinal cord injury (SCI) affects millions of people worldwide, resulting in persistent direct and secondary effects including but not limited to motor, sensory, and autonomic dysfunction. The widespread nature of this condition, as well as its detrimental effects, makes recovery following SCI an important clinical problem. One primary issue identified in SCI among other neurological conditions is fibrotic scarring, as its dynamic nature provides both beneficial and detrimental effects over its developmental course. Initially, early scar formation contributes to wound closure and tissue stabilization, but chronic, persistent fibrosis later interferes with axonal growth and other neural repair mechanisms. The scar itself is highly dynamic, consisting of components including collagens, fibronectin, proteoglycans, and laminins, all of which have diverse localization and functionality throughout scar maturation. Its formation is regulated by various signaling mechanisms, including inflammatory signaling, profibrotic pathways, vascular responses, interactions between fibroblasts and neighboring cells, and changes in the specific mechanical environment of the injury site. This review focuses primarily on SCI, with findings from additional central nervous system injury and disease models used to provide a holistic, clinically relevant overview of fibrotic scar organization, profibrotic signaling, and potential therapeutic targets.

papers.title: Angiotensin II-Induced Cardiac Fibrosis: Genomic and Molecular Drivers, Emerging Biomarkers and Therapeutic Perspectives.
papers.abstract: Chronically elevated angiotensin II (Ang II) drives adverse cardiac remodelling, converting a reparative response into progressive interstitial and perivascular fibrosis that stiffens the ventricle and precedes overt heart failure. Acting through the angiotensin II type 1 receptor, Ang II generates reactive oxygen species, recruits and polarises immune cells and activates resident fibroblasts, converging on transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β)-dependent and mechanotransductive programmes that drive myofibroblast differentiation and excessive extracellular matrix (ECM) deposition. The magnitude of this response varies between patients: germline variation in renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) genes, loci for heart failure and imaging-defined fibrosis, epigenomic reprogramming of the fibroblast, non-coding RNA networks and metabolic rewiring of collagen-producing cells all modulate the transition from compensated hypertrophy to fibrotic failure. This review integrates these genomic, epigenomic, transcriptomic and metabolomic layers with the signalling architecture of Ang II-induced fibrosis, and reviews the circulating biomarkers-collagen turnover peptides, matricellular and immune mediators, non-coding RNAs and cell-free DNA methylation signatures-that could detect fibrotic activity before remodelling becomes irreversible. We then consider why fibrosis regression under RAAS blockade appears heterogeneous, which emerging targets are mechanistically credible, and how genotype-biomarker-imaging phenotyping could enrich antifibrotic trials. Priorities for ancestrally diverse cohorts and standardised biomarker methodology are identified.

papers.title: OncoSpot enables benchmarking of cancer spatial transcriptomics methods across tumor evolutionary modes
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) is increasingly used to map clonal architecture within tumors, yet methods for analyzing cancer ST data are difficult to evaluate because real tumors lack ground truth for copy-number alterations (CNAs), subclonal identity, and malignant cell fraction. papers.title: Unified cell segmentation for spatial transcriptomics via transcript reassignment
papers.abstract: High-resolution spatial transcriptomics (ST) measures gene expression as individually localized molecules on imaging-based platforms or as counts in subcellular bins on sequencing-based platforms, and both must be assigned to cells before cell-level analysis. papers.title: Single-cell and spatial transcriptomic insights into neural substrates of behavioural dysfunction in Alzheimer's disease.
papers.abstract: The transition from bulk-tissue profiling to single-cell and spatially resolved transcriptomics has reshaped our understanding of Alzheimer's disease (AD) from a passive proteinopathy to a coordinated multicellular process spanning the neurovascular unit. This review synthesizes the multicellular landscape of AD, tracing how cell-state-specific remodelling drives network collapse and cognitive decline. Neuronally, selective vulnerability targets projection networks and subclass-specific inhibitory interneurons. Their transcriptional silencing compromises projection pathways, including the entorhinal-hippocampal perforant path, disrupts cortical microcircuits, and underlies episodic memory impairment, hyperexcitability, and executive control failure. This neuronal degeneration is dynamically coupled to reactive glial and vascular remodelling across distinct spatial niches. We examine the non-linear transition of homeostatic astrocytes and microglia into specialized, plaque-associated reactive sub-states, as well as paracrine signalling decay at the neurovascular interface. Compromised capillary tight junctions and the shedding of pericytic survival receptors are proposed to promote blood-brain barrier disintegrity, triggering a feed-forward neuroinflammatory cascade of complement-mediated synaptic pruning. Crucially, we establish a three-tiered hierarchy of evidence, rigorously distinguishing cross-sectional, associative human postmortem findings from inferred functional trajectories in human cellular platforms, and causal, perturbation-based validations in transgenic rodent models. We review how contemporary multi-scale integration-combining single-nucleus transcriptomics with functional electrophysiological platforms and biophysical connectomic modelling-bridges the gap between terminal postmortem signatures and living brain dynamics. Finally, we outline a coordinated translational roadmap illustrating how spatially resolved cell-state networks can guide the development of fluid and imaging biomarkers, support biologically informed patient stratification, enrich clinical trials, and accelerate the development of circuit-restoring precision therapies, thereby providing a mechanistic framework that links cell-state transitions to neural circuit dysfunction, behavioural impairment, and precision medicine in Alzheimer's disease.

papers.title: Platform Switching with Dental Implants: What Have We Learned Over the Past 20 Years?
papers.abstract: Since its formal description in 2006, platform switching has evolved from a single clinical obser-vation into a widely investigated technique and a recognized design feature in implant dentistry. The effect requires establishing the platform-switched configuration at the placement of a heal-ing abutment and maintaining it thereafter. It proposes framing the implant-abutment interface as a biologic boundary, identifies unresolved questions after 20 years, and outlines directions for future research.

papers.title: Enhancing cell type deconvolution in spatial transcriptomics through incorporating multiple reference panels.
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) captures gene expression with spatial context but often at resolutions where each spatial location contains multiple cells. Deconvolution of cell-type proportions is therefore essential, yet existing methods typically rely on a single scRNA-seq reference, limiting accuracy when references are incomplete or mismatched especially in complex tissues. These limitations highlight the need for a framework that can integrate multiple references while leveraging spatial information. We introduce SWIMR (Spatially Weighted Integration for Multi-Reference deconvolution), a statistical framework that integrates multiple scRNA-seq references while accounting for spatial correlations. SWIMR models each spatial location as a weighted combination of references, with both cell-type proportions and reference weights varying across tissue locations. Across comprehensive simulations and diverse ST datasets, SWIMR consistently outperformed single-reference approaches. In developing human heart tissue, it recovered ground-truth cell-type compositions with the highest accuracy. In mouse embryo and liver cancer, it leveraged context-specific references to resolve organ-specific cell types and increase sensitivity for biologically relevant pathways. Together, these results establish SWIMR as a robust framework for multi-reference deconvolution in spatial transcriptomics.

papers.abstract: Diabetes mellitus increases the risk and severity of periodontitis by disrupting periodontal mucosa homeostasis and promoting sustained chronic inflammation. papers.title: An Infusible Decellularized Extracellular Matrix Material Binds to Vasculature in Infarcted Myocardium and Induces Pro-Reparative Gene Expression Following Acute Myocardial Infarction Through Inherent Avidity and Bioactive Signaling.
papers.abstract: To treat acute myocardial infarction (MI), we previously engineered an infusible decellularized extracellular matrix (iECM) biomaterial that reduces vascular permeability and exerts immunomodulatory and pro-reparative effects. To probe the heterogenous contents of iECM and its contribution to infarct localization and downstream biological function, we separated iECM into high and low molecular weight (MW) components. Though mass spectrometry showed similar compositions, biochemical analysis and transmission electron microscopy revealed higher sGAG content within the nanofibrillar high MW, while the globular low MW had more exposed functional groups. These differences translated to a higher binding efficiency of the high MW to ECM proteins and cell surface receptors under flow, while the low MW drove the reduction in vascular permeability. Neither component alone achieved the infarct retention levels of complete iECM, showing that the two components exhibit dependent infarct localization and both are necessary for iECM's overall function. Via single‑nucleus RNA sequencing, both components elicited comparable immunomodulatory and pro‑reparative transcriptional profiles, suggesting that the similarity in composition likely drives the transcriptional response. These findings elucidate the material properties of an intravascularly deliverable ECM biomaterial and how those properties relate to downstream biological behavior, enabling future work investigating nanomaterial mimicry and improvements in material processing and potency.

papers.title: LANCE-seq: Live-tissue Analysis via Needle-encoded Capture Extraction for Spatial Transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics enables the resolution of spatial heterogeneity in gene expression within tissues, yet most existing sequencing-based methods rely on ex vivo tissue processing, making it difficult to track dynamic molecular changes in the same living individual. We developed LANCE-seq (Live-tissue Analysis via Needle-encoded Capture Extraction sequencing), a live-tissue spatial transcriptomics platform based on encoded microneedle arrays that enables high-density spatial RNA capture through poly(amidoamine) (PAMAM) dendrimer-functionalized interfaces and microfluidic orthogonal combinatorial encoding. In frozen mouse brain tissue, LANCE-seq detected an average of 6,399 genes per spatial spot and reconstructed the spatial distribution of major brain regions and representative marker genes. Furthermore, in the acetaminophen (APAP)-induced acute liver injury model, LANCE-seq enabled repeated sampling from the same living animal at different time points. At 6 h after APAP treatment, injury-related genes such as Hmox1 , Ddit3 , Atf3 , and Fgf21 were significantly elevated, and transcriptional programs associated with stress, inflammation, and cellular injury were broadly enhanced. Meanwhile, liver zonation-related transcriptional signatures were remodeled, with different relative zonation states all exhibiting activation of injury programs. By integrating high-throughput spatial encoding with minimally invasive in vivo sampling, LANCE-seq provides a platform for longitudinal spatial transcriptomic studies of drug responses and disease progression.

papers.title: CIRCA learns identifiable cell- and niche-level programs and their interactions with tissue pathology from spatial transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Interactions among cells and their local microenvironments shape tissue organization and function, while their dysregulation can contribute to disease. In Alzheimer’s disease (AD), the complex responses of glial cells and neurons to amyloid-β pathology can both mitigate and exacerbate neuronal injury. Spatial transcriptomics enables investigation of these relationships in situ , but recovering interpretable transcriptional programs and their interactions from spatial transcriptomics remains challenging, in part because conventional nonlinear models are non-identifiable. Here we present CIRCA (Causal Interaction Representation for Cellular Architectures), a self-supervised causal representation learning framework that jointly learns identifiable cell- and neighborhood-level transcriptional programs and the directed interactions among them under explicit assumptions. It can also be extended to incorporate additional modalities such as pathology. Benchmarked against five existing methods across seven cell-resolution datasets, CIRCA achieved the highest biological accuracy in six and the highest overall score in all five multi-section datasets, while recovering higher-order anatomical organization. In an AD mouse model, incorporating amyloid-β pathology revealed four region-specific plaque niches enriched for microglia. Plaque-associated microglia shared a core disease-associated response whose strength varied by region, and AD genetic risk was preferentially enriched in hippocampal and cortical plaque-associated microglia. Reproducible latent factors linked to cell-level amyloid burden separated phagocytic from inflammatory microglial programs. Applied to a human colorectal cancer dataset, CIRCA resolved patient-specific tumor niches, conserved stromal remodeling niches, and distinct macrophage states, highlighting its versatility. Together, these results establish CIRCA as a methodological advance over existing approaches, enabling deeper insights into tissue organization and the molecular dependencies linking cells to their local environments.

papers.title: Multimodal population-scale cell atlases define archetypes and extremes of human blood
papers.abstract: The cellular composition of blood is fundamental to human physiology and is routinely measured to assess health and disease. Circulating immune cells show extensive heterogeneity, but the organising principles and extremes of variation across individuals remain undefined. Here, using single-cell transcriptomics across two biobank cohorts encompassing [~]6,000 individuals, we show that human blood occupies recurrent archetypal states defined by coordinated cell composition patterns. We delineate three major archetypes spanning naive lymphoid, myeloid and cytotoxic composition, and two minor archetypes characterised by type I interferon-driven inflammation and expanded premalignant CD5+ B cells. We develop cell2clone to infer lymphocyte clonal expansions, revealing how reactive clonal processes drive the cytotoxic archetype and premalignant clonal expansion establishes the CD5+ B cell archetype, creating outlier states that uncover context-specific effects of germline variants. Clonal haematopoiesis and mosaic chromosomal alterations influence blood states in an archetype-dependent manner. The archetype framework links blood states to common disease risk and clinical blood counts and, through a machine-learning model ArcheTypist, classifies infection and cancer immunotherapy outcomes. This population-scale framework has implications for diagnostics, early disease detection, immunotherapy stratification and mechanistic insights into disease susceptibility and therapy response, providing an organising model for identifying compositional subtypes across human tissues.

papers.title: Single-cell dissection of immune-state architecture across diverse human population cohorts
papers.abstract: The extension of human lifespan is accompanied by a growing burden of chronic disease and multimorbidity. The immune system, whose functional state is continuously remodelled by ageing, environmental exposures, infection history and disease, is pivotal to respond to these challenges. However, how these factors jointly influence immune variation, regulatory mechanisms and disease susceptibility across populations remains poorly understood. Here we present an outline and first results of the CARDINAL (Cellular Architecture of immune-state Regulation, Disease, and Immune Networks across the Adult Lifecourse) project. We generated a new population-scale single-cell atlas of peripheral blood comprising almost 10 million immune cells from 6,003 individuals across two UK cohorts with integrated genomic and longitudinal electronic health record data: the UK Biobank (predominantly European ancestry British) and Genes & Health (British Bangladeshi and British Pakistani). We identify immune-state architectures, shared across cohorts, associated with ageing, chronic viral exposure, inflammatory activation and premalignant conditions. We show that demographic and lifestyle factors induce largely conserved immune programmes, while chronic cardiometabolic diseases are associated with cohort-dominant cellular programmes and transcriptional states. Disentangling of genetic and clinical influences reveals coordinated regulatory programmes associated with metabolic, inflammatory and infectious remodelling. These programmes are observed in specific disease contexts and immune states, such as those induced by chronic viral exposure, often independently of genetic differences. Together, our findings support a model of immune-state architecture shaped by ageing, environment, disease history and genetic variation, which can be read from population-specific regulatory landscapes.

papers.title: Hierarchical genetic regulatory architecture of the human immune system informs complex disease mechanisms
papers.abstract: How inherited genetic variation propagates through multicellular regulatory systems to influence human disease remains poorly understood. To reconstruct the regulatory architecture of genetic variation on circulating immune cells, we analysed single-cell transcriptomes from 6.7 million peripheral blood mononuclear cells from 4,452 European-ancestry UK Biobank participants, identifying 114,063 independent cis-regulatory effects affecting 15,419 genes. Using a new statistical workflow (FLANDERS), we map the hierarchical organisation of these effects and the underlying regulatory architecture across tissues, immune lineages, cell types and cell states. We find that disease-associated variants predominantly act through regulatory programmes shared within immune lineages and broad cellular compartments, rather than through highly specific cellular states. We show that local cis-regulatory effects commonly act through coherent regulatory pathways implicating transcription factor cascades and intercellular signalling, which allows linking together multiple disease genes. We demonstrate independent support for these genes and mechanisms through rare variant associations. Our findings reveal a highly organised structure of immune regulatory variation shaping human disease, and provide a highly effective framework for interpreting disease associations and prioritising therapeutic targets.

papers.title: Circulating immune architecture across age, exposures and disease in ethnically diverse UK cohorts.
papers.abstract: Human immune composition reflects genetic background and cumulative life-course exposures, yet how these influences shape immune architecture across populations and disease remains poorly understood. Here we integrate single-cell transcriptomics, matched clinical haematology and electronic health records from 5,079 individuals of European, British-Pakistani and British-Bangladeshi ancestries to quantify 26 circulating immune cell types and 62 transcriptional states. We map immune compositional variation associated with age, sex, adiposity and smoking, revealing distinct patterns across adulthood and associations between modifiable exposures and advanced immune age. Across common diseases, immune compositional signatures converge on recurrent inflammatory myeloid, adaptive-memory and interferon programmes, whose expression varies with age and population context. Cardiovascular therapies are associated with selective shifts in disease-associated immune states. Immune composition further discriminates common cardiometabolic diseases and resolves patients into endotypes with distinct metabolic and clinical profiles. These findings establish circulating immune architecture as an integrative phenotype linking life-course exposures, population context and disease, providing a framework for precision population immunology.

papers.title: Stigma and unsupportive disclosure reactions are associated with elevated depressive symptom burden among adolescent mothers in Juja Sub-County, Kenya: a community-based cross-sectional study
papers.abstract: Girls who become pregnant during adolescence in sub-Saharan Africa carry a high burden of depressive symptoms. Kenyan studies have relied on antenatal clinic samples and have not looked at stigma, the response to pregnancy disclosure and economic circumstances in the same analysis. We assessed how these factors relate to depressive symptom burden among adolescent mothers in Juja Sub-County, Kiambu County. We surveyed 227 girls who had been pregnant or given birth at 10-19 years, drawn by stratified random sampling from a line list of 466 mapped across five wards. Trained assistants administered a structured questionnaire covering background characteristics, pregnancy and disclosure, stigma, and a seven-item depressive symptom checklist. Elevated symptom burden was set in advance at four or more endorsed items. Two logistic regression models examined factors linked to stigma (n = 199) and to elevated symptom burden (n = 184). Of those with parity data, 194 of 197 had already given birth. Most respondents were 17-19 years old (86.8%) and single (69.2%), 92.5% had no income of their own, and 47.1% had left school early. Nine in ten pregnancies (91.2%) were unplanned, and 41.4% of girls met anger, rejection or indifference when they first disclosed. Stigma was reported by 43.2%, elevated symptom burden by 27.1% and thoughts of self-harm by 16.4%. Only 27.3% had attended any support programme. Being single was the one factor associated with stigma (adjusted odds ratio [AOR] 3.50; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.48-8.31). Elevated symptom burden was associated with stigma (AOR 3.21; 1.54-6.69) and with an unsupportive disclosure reaction (AOR 2.54; 1.19-5.41), and was less likely with each additional year of age (AOR 0.69; 0.49-0.96). Programme attendance showed no association (AOR 0.89; 0.41-1.94). In this peri-urban community, depressive symptoms clustered among adolescent mothers who had been stigmatised or poorly received when they disclosed their pregnancy, and stigma tracked marital status more closely than poverty. Screening with validated tools at postnatal, child-health and antenatal visits, guidance for families and partners on responding to disclosure, and community work on attitudes to unmarried motherhood deserve testing in this setting.

papers.title: LIFE-seq: longitudinal spatial transcriptomics of living tissue
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) has deepened our understanding of cellular spatial heterogeneity, yet existing technologies are predominantly confined to fixed or frozen specimens, limiting longitudinal molecular profiling of the same living tissue. To overcome this limitation, we developed LIFE-seq (Living-tissue in situ nanoforest extraction for spatiotemporal transcriptomic mapping), a minimally invasive approach that combines high-density nanoforest arrays for molecular sampling with directed transfer onto spatially barcoded messenger RNA (mRNA) capture chips. LIFE-seq enables spatial transcriptomic profiling while preserving overall tissue integrity and provides a modular strategy with the potential to integrate different 3’-end capture platforms. Performance validation demonstrated high concordance in global transcriptomic profiles and spatial gene expression patterns between nanoforest-derived replicas and conventional tissue sections, as well as faithful recapitulation of pathological features in a traumatic brain injury (TBI) model. Furthermore, longitudinal spatial transcriptomic profiling of cortical injury in the same mouse revealed temporally distinct injury responses, progressive activation of immune-associated gene programs, and spatially heterogeneous cell-type-specific expression changes. By enabling repeated molecular sampling and spatial transcriptomic analysis of living tissue, LIFE-seq provides a versatile framework for investigating tissue dynamics and pathological progression in vivo .

papers.title: ZNF683-positive tissue-resident memory T cells organize treatment-refractory niches with targetable circuits in inclusion body myositis
papers.abstract: Inclusion body myositis (IBM) is a progressive autoimmune myositis refractory to conventional immunosuppression, yet mechanisms sustaining chronic inflammation remain unresolved. Trajectory analysis positioned an early-disease ZBTB16+ cytotoxic T cell state upstream of ZNF683+IL7R+TRM. Ligand-receptor modeling nominated candidate targetable circuits involving IL-15-IL15RA, XCL1-XCR1, and HMGB1/CXCL12-CXCR4. Spatial transcriptomics localized ZNF683+TRM to stress-associated IBM niches. These findings define a disease-specific TRM-centered circuit linked to treatment refractoriness and candidate therapeutic vulnerabilities in IBM.
