papers.title: Three-dimensional reconstruction of ultrasound imaging in dentistry: a systematic review.
papers.abstract: BackgroundThree-dimensional ultrasound (3D-US) reconstruction has emerged as a potential solution to the limited field of view and operator dependence of two-dimensional intraoral ultrasonography. Multiple acquisition, tracking, and reconstruction strategies have been proposed, yet no prior systematic review has synthesized the methods used specifically within dentistry.ObjectiveTo identify and compare 3D-US reconstruction techniques applied in dentistry and evaluate how acquisition strategy, spatial tracking, and reconstruction methodology influence accuracy, reproducibility, feasibility, and clinical applicability.MethodsA systematic search of 5 databases was performed. Studies were included in the review if they used ultrasound imaging with any 3D-US reconstruction method for a defined dental application. Risk of bias was assessed using a customized hybrid QUADAS-2/QUIN/STARD framework.ResultsThirteen studies (2010-2025) met the inclusion criteria; 10 were in vitro and 3 in vivo. Acquisition methods included mechanized linear-stage scanning (n = 6), robotic arm control (n = 2), tracked freehand (n = 2), untracked freehand (n = 1), and custom intraoral jigs (n = 2). Accuracy ranged from 12 to 50 μm for digital impressions to sub-millimeter deviations for periodontal and ridge assessments, with most error rates below 10%. Reproducibility and clinical feasibility were both inversely related to hardware complexity: mechanized and robotic systems achieved the highest precision and enabled precise positioning for repeated evaluations; however, they had the lowest clinical usability. Conversely, freehand approaches demonstrated the strongest clinical potential but at the expense of reproducible positioning and highly precise measurements. Risk of bias was high or unclear in all studies due to heterogeneity, small sample sizes, and limited in vivo validation.ConclusionsOver 15 years, 3D-US reconstruction in dentistry has advanced substantially, demonstrating promising accuracy for digital impressions, periodontal assessment, ridge measurement, and implant planning. However, most studies remain feasibility-based and in vitro, and methodological variation limits comparability. Future progress will depend on standardization of validation frameworks, increased in vivo accuracy studies, and development of compact, automated acquisition workflows. With continued refinement, 3D-US has the potential to become a clinically practical, radiation-free imaging modality for diagnostic and procedural applications in dentistry.

papers.title: A biological approach for corticoperiosteal free flaps in mandibular reconstruction without rigid fixation: the wrapping technique.
papers.abstract: Mandibular reconstruction in irradiated or otherwise compromised bone environments requires both mechanical stability and biological revitalization of devitalized tissue. Corticoperiosteal flaps from the medial femoral condyle provide a thin, vascularized osteogenic interface particularly suited to restoring bone vitality in limited mandibular defects, but their effectiveness depends on stable fixation and intimate periosteal contact, both of which may be compromised by postoperative edema or the use of rigid hardware. This technical note describes a biological approach combining press-fit seating of the cortical component within a prepared mandibular recess and a circumferential periosteal wrapping technique that offers hardware-free stability and continuous vascularized coverage of exposed bone surfaces. The method involves a non-interruptive mandibulectomy with shaping of a three-dimensional mandibular recess, harvest of the corticoperiosteal flap with preservation of the cambium layer, and placement of pre-positioned sutures to allow wrapping without manipulating the vascular pedicle. The vascularized periosteum is then drawn around the superior mandibular margin and secured to create a watertight biological envelope. This approach aims to optimize osseous integration, reduce hardware-related complications, and enhance revascularization in irradiated, infected, or osteonecrotic bone. The technique may be particularly relevant in non-interruptive oncologic mandibulectomies requiring postoperative radiotherapy and may be extended to other periosteal flaps for small or localized mandibular defects. This hardware-free, biologically oriented method provides a simple and effective option for selected mandibular reconstructions.

papers.title: Weighted co-expression reveals early circadian and metabolic dysregulation in precystic kidneys.
papers.abstract: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) initiates long before cysts appear, yet the molecular triggers of this precystic phase remain poorly defined. Early upregulated modules showed activation of circadian regulators (Bmal1/Arntl, Per1, Per3, Npas2) and sterol biosynthesis under Srebf2 control, whereas mitochondrial and oxidative-phosphorylation modules were markedly repressed. Transcription-factor enrichment revealed distinct regulatory axes: circadian control by BMAL1, metabolic regulation through SREBP2 (encoded by Srebf2), and inflammatory/cytokine signaling mediated by STAT3, p53, and NF-κB. These regulatory programs diverged transcriptionally within two weeks of Pkd1 loss, establishing an epithelial-driven phase characterized by circadian misalignment, metabolic rewiring, mitochondrial suppression and concomitant low-level inflammatory signaling. Inflammatory and stress-response modules intensified during later cystic stages. Notably, Pkd2 clustered within a small but transcriptionally active high-ranked module suggesting early perturbation of the polycystin complex. Together, these data define precystic ADPKD as a convergence of independent epithelial programs accompanied by early inflammatory engagement that precedes overt cyst expansion, providing a modular framework for early biomarker discovery and therapeutic targeting.

papers.title: Spontaneous neuropathic pain.
papers.abstract: AbstractSpontaneous pain is a highly prevalent and disabling consequence of neuropathic disorders, yet it remains mechanistically underdefined and therapeutically underserved. Historically, preclinical animal models and clinical trials have been overwhelmingly biased toward stimulus-evoked hypersensitivity, relegating spontaneous pain to a secondary manifestation. Emerging evidence now challenges this view. Converging data from pharmacology, neural recordings, and systems-level causal manipulations indicate that spontaneous and stimulus-evoked pain arise from substantially dissociable molecular, cellular, and circuit substrates. Injured-fiber-derived ectopic activity within specific sensory neuron subtypes serves as a dominant peripheral generator of spontaneous pain, whereas cellularly distinct, intact spared-fiber pathways mediate stimulus-evoked hypersensitivity. At spinal and supraspinal levels, spontaneous pain preferentially engages affective-salience networks during pain chronification and may ultimately become stabilized within higher-order circuitry-while remaining dynamically coupled to afferent input. This mechanistic delineation carries critical translational implications. Current diagnostic and treatment guidelines rarely differentiate symptom domains, and most therapies have been validated primarily using stimulus-evoked or overall pain intensity endpoints-potentially contributing to a mechanism-therapy mismatch and variable efficacy. We argue that spontaneous neuropathic pain should be defined as a separate symptom domain rather than considered as a spontaneous manifestation of evoked pain mechanisms. This recognition demands longitudinal, biomarker-informed phenotyping to capture its persistent and fluctuating nature, and thereby enable robust mechanistic dissection at peripheral, spinal, and cortical nodes. Reframing spontaneous neuropathic pain along these lines will provide a foundation for precision therapeutics that target defined cell types, specific molecular drivers, and maladaptive network states-enabling mechanism-based, symptom-aligned treatments.

papers.title: Spatial determinants of pathological complete response and residual disease after neoadjuvant therapy in breast cancer.
papers.abstract: Pathological complete response (pCR) after neoadjuvant therapy is associated with favorable outcomes in breast cancer, yet differences in response cannot be explained by immune-cell abundance alone. An effective antitumor response requires coordinated immune recruitment, local activation and renewal, movement across tissue boundaries, contact with malignant cells, and maintenance of effector function. Disruption at any stage may preserve resistant tumor regions despite substantial overall immune infiltration. Current evidence indicates that immune-cell positioning, multicellular organization, and the spatial distribution of stromal, vascular, and metabolic constraints can provide information beyond conventional cell-density measurements. However, the strength and clinical meaning of these associations vary according to breast cancer subtype, treatment regimen, sampling time point, and analytical platform. Pretreatment tissue, early on-treatment samples, and surgical residual disease address distinct baseline response-associated, pharmacodynamic, and prognostic questions and should therefore be interpreted separately. Residual disease represents a treatment-selected ecosystem rather than simply a smaller version of the untreated tumor. We integrate available evidence into a time-resolved framework linking baseline spatial architecture, treatment-related remodeling, residual disease organization, and subsequent clinical outcome. Translation into clinical practice will require standardized spatial definitions and measurements, reproducible assessment of organized immune structures, subtype- and regimen-specific validation, and demonstration of added value beyond established pathological indicators. Spatially resolved analysis may improve understanding of heterogeneous neoadjuvant responses and support more precise post-treatment risk assessment.

papers.title: Clinical and Psychological Impact of Pruritus Related to Skin Barrier Damage.

papers.title: Force-torque classification of reference-profile-defined drilling states during robot-assisted dental implant osteotomy.
papers.abstract: To evaluate whether force-torque features can classify three predefined, reference-profile-defined operational drilling states during robot-assisted implant osteotomy under specimen-level separation. Axial force (Fz) and drilling torque (Mz) were sampled at 1000 Hz, segmented into 100 ms windows with a 50 ms step, and represented by 42 time-, frequency-, and wavelet-domain features; 23 features were selected using training-only ANOVA ranking and correlation pruning. Specimens were separated into training, validation, and held-out test sets (18/6/6). Linear support vector machine (SVM), random forest (RF), and XGBoost were evaluated against predefined depth-indexed operational reference profiles; a same-acquisition CBCT rule served as an imaging comparator. The dataset contained 92 675 overlapping windows. On six held-out specimens (36 osteotomies; 18 496 windows), XGBoost achieved 93.0% accuracy (specimen-clustered 95% CI, 92.0%-94.0%), 82.9% balanced accuracy, and 85.6% macro-F1. RF and SVM accuracies were 90.5% and 88.8%, respectively. The CBCT rule achieved 92.3% accuracy but lower balanced accuracy (80.1%) and transitional recall (51.1%). XGBoost transitional recall was 59.6%, increasing to 73.0% in a weighted sensitivity configuration at the cost of lower overall accuracy. Accuracy decreased from 94.1% away from class boundaries to 75.6% in boundary-adjacent windows. Force-torque features differentiated the three predefined reference-profile-defined drilling states under specimen-separated evaluation. XGBoost achieved the highest classification performance, with errors concentrated primarily in transitional and boundary-adjacent windows.

papers.title: Manufacturing Route-Dependent Biointerface Modulation in 3D-Printed and Conventional Dental Implant Systems.
papers.abstract: Implant manufacturing routes determine surface architecture and, consequently, modulate biointerface interactions that govern early biological responses. Although additive manufacturing has emerged as a promising alternative to conventional subtractive techniques, direct comparisons among commercially available systems remain limited. In this study, a commercially available additively manufactured dental implant was compared with four market-available conventionally machined systems to elucidate manufacturing route-dependent biointerface modulation. Physicochemical properties, surface topography, and electrochemical behavior were evaluated alongside biological responses. Protein adsorption profiles were characterized by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS), while polymicrobial accumulation was quantified and profiled. Microbially induced surface degradation was assessed by titanium ion release. The additively manufactured implant and the market-leading conventional system exhibited higher surface roughness and distinctive topographical features, which were associated with reduced polymicrobial biofilm accumulation, lower titanium ion release following microbial challenge, and stable electrochemical behavior. Although conventionally machined implants exhibited broader proteomic profiles, functional enrichment analyses revealed overlapping biological categories among implant systems. Collectively, the findings demonstrate that the manufacturing route critically modulates implant biointerface characteristics, with additive manufacturing achieving performance comparable to established commercial systems.

papers.abstract: Background and aimsResmetirom has emerged as a major advance in MASH pharmacotherapy as the first approved liver-targeted THR-β agonist; however, variable therapeutic efficacy and adverse responses may limit its clinical benefits. papers.title: Extracellular Matrix Remodeling in Tumors: Forces beyond Fibroblasts.
papers.abstract: Aberrant extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling in tumors is characterized by altered deposition, enzymatic cross-linking, degradation, and organization of matrix molecules that in turn can contribute directly to tumor invasiveness, immune evasion, and resistance to therapy. Traditionally, cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAF) have been considered the principal architects of ECM remodeling in tumors. However, the role of non-fibroblast cell populations in modulating ECM structure and function and how these processes intersect with immune regulation, metabolism, and metastasis are also crucial but currently underappreciated. Challenging the prevailing fibroblast-centric paradigm, this review provides an overview of how non-fibroblast cell types engage in dynamic cross-talk and collectively shape the biochemical and biomechanical landscape of tumors. Therapeutic strategies targeting these alternative stromal players could disrupt protumor ECM dynamics, enhance antitumor immunity, and restore tissue homeostasis. Thus, a comprehensive understanding of the intricate network of non-fibroblast stromal cells within the tumor microenvironment (TME) can help elucidate opportunities for precision medicine and personalized cancer care, leading to the development of innovative therapeutic interventions targeting the TME.

papers.title: Serial Casting as a Conservative Treatment for Adults With Upper Extremity Burn Contractures: A Prospective Longitudinal Study With a Criterion for Change.
papers.abstract: Joint contractures and hypertrophic scars (HSc) are common complications following burn injuries, significantly impairing range of motion (ROM) and quality of life. While conservative interventions target either contractures or HSc, serial casting (SC) is typically reserved for patients who fail traditional therapy or are nonadherent. The purpose of this study was to estimate the extent to which ROM (regular and revised passive and active), scar characteristics (objective and subjective), and patient-reported upper extremity (UE) function change following an individually tailored SC treatment program after switching from a minimum of 3 days of usual care. This study employed a prospective longitudinal intervention design with a criterion for change. Participants with UE joint passive ROM (PROM) loss of > 15% were included. Measures were taken at baseline, pre-SC, every Monday and Friday thereafter, and 3 weeks after casting. The QuickDASH and Patient Scar Assessment Scale were evaluated at baseline and 3 weeks after casting. Eleven individuals (13 joints) were included in this study. Regular PROM, revised PROM, and active ROM and scar thickness improvements were statistically significant. Participants reported improvements in UE function for 11/13 joints (median 16%, range 9%-21%) and scar impression for all scars (median 6, 4-10). Participants also perceived that SC reduced their rehabilitation burden. In conclusion, when possible, SC should be prioritized to increase PROM, reduce HSc thickness, and enhance patient-perceived UE function and scar outcomes.

papers.title: Ultrasound-based estimation of periodontal probing depth using category-specific supracrestal tissue attachment calibration.
papers.abstract: ObjectiveTo determine category-specific supracrestal tissue attachment (STA) dimensions and apply these values to calibrate high-frequency ultrasound-derived measurements to match clinical probing depth (PD), and to examine the reliability of ultrasound landmark annotation in healthy and diseased cohorts.MethodsIntraoral high-frequency ultrasound (40 MHz) imaging was performed to acquire images from 34 subjects (20 healthy and 14 with stage II-IV periodontitis). Four trained raters annotated 955 teeth for the gingival margin (GM), cementoenamel junction (CEJ), and alveolar bone crest (ABC). The image-based gingival height (iGH) was defined as the distance from the GM to the average bone crest. Ultrasound assessment is in terms of distances to the bone crest, whereas PD is measured to the STA. Ultrasound measurements were calibrated using category-specific STA values to estimate PD. Method agreement between iPD and clinical PD was evaluated via Bland-Altman analysis using a ±1 mm clinical acceptance limit. This prospective calibration-validation study (34 subjects; 955 annotated tooth-surface observations) compared high-frequency ultrasound-derived measurements with conventional clinical periodontal PD measurements. The dataset was partitioned into a calibration set (721 observations, 27 subjects) and an independent validation set (234 observations, 7 subjects).ResultsInter- and intra-rater reliability was high, with correlation coefficients ranging from 0.894 to 0.998. Calibrated STA values ranged from 1.349 mm for molar-buccal to 2.970 mm for anterior-buccal teeth, yielding an overall mean of 2.162 ± 0.549 mm that falls within established histological reference ranges. The observed level of agreement lies within the reported inter-examiner variability of conventional periodontal probing.Advances in knowledgeThis study represents the initial comprehensive characterization of STA for all tooth types and surfaces by means of high-frequency ultrasound, which illustrates that calibration for each of these tooth type groups is essential for accurate estimation of PD. This approach may provide a noninvasive adjunct to periodontal probing assessment.

papers.title: A PTX3/TLR4 axis sustains sonic hedgehog-medulloblastoma growth and defines a new therapeutic vulnerability.
papers.abstract: BackgroundSonic hedgehog-medulloblastoma (SHH-MB) represents a biologically diverse and clinically challenging subgroup, especially in high-risk variants characterized by metastatic dissemination. Despite progress in molecular stratification, current treatments rely on intensive multimodal regimens that are associated with substantial long-term neurotoxicity. Identifying novel oncogenic mechanisms that can be therapeutically exploited is therefore a critical priority.MethodsWe combined transcriptomic analyses of patient datasets with immunohistochemistry, RNAscope, and protein profiling to evaluate PTX3 expression in MB subgroups. Functional studies were performed in SHH-MB cell lines following PTX3 knockdown or knockout. Effects on proliferation, migration, and angiogenesis were assessed through multiple in vitro assays. In vivo relevance was tested using subcutaneous and orthotopic xenograft models. Mechanistic insights were obtained through phospho-kinase arrays, Western blotting, and GSEA. A high-throughput drug screen and combination studies with specific inhibitors and standard chemotherapy (vincristine/cisplatin/cyclophosphamide; VCC) were performed to assess therapeutic potential.ResultsOur results reveal that PTX3 was strongly enriched in SHH-MB subgroup, where it supported proliferation, motility, and angiogenesis. Mechanistically, PTX3 activated a TLR4-dependent IRAK1/PI3K-Akt/GSK-3/β-catenin signaling cascade. Genetic downregulation or pharmacologic blockade of PTX3-TLR4 significantly reduced tumor growth and angiogenesis in vivo. Moreover, the TLR4 inhibitor TAK-242 markedly impacted SHH-MB growth in vitro, and combination therapy of TAK-242 and VCC produced additive/synergistic effects in vitro and significantly prolonged survival in orthotopic SHH-MB-bearing mice.ConclusionsOur findings identify PTX3-TLR4 signaling as key oncogenic driver and a promising therapeutic -vulnerability in SHH-MB. Targeting this pathway enhances the efficacy of standard therapy and represents a rationale for mechanism-based combination strategies.

papers.title: Quantification of supracrestal tissue attachment using high-frequency ultrasound.
papers.abstract: ObjectivesTo develop and validate a noninvasive ultrasound (US)-based framework for quantifying supracrestal tissue attachment (STA) and evaluating tooth-type variation in STA dimensions, to assess the accuracy of conventional periodontal probing against photographic ground truth (GT), and US images.MethodsA high-frequency, miniaturized side-facing US transducer was used to simultaneously image gingival soft tissue, alveolar bone, and periodontal probes. Ex vivo swine jaws were imaged to compare US-derived probing depth and STA measurements with GT photographic measurements and conventional manual probing. Measurement bias and agreement were evaluated using statistical analyses. Observed anatomical trends were further examined using full-mouth human cadaver imaging and validated in vivo in human subjects. Power analysis was performed to determine sensitivity for detecting biologically relevant differences between tooth types.ResultsUltrasound-derived probing depth measurements showed lower bias (0.23 ± 0.42 mm) relative to GT than manual probing (0.54 ± 0.25 mm) and enabled direct visualization of STA with a periodontal probe. Agreement analyses showed improved accuracy of US measurements compared with conventional probing. Systematic differences in STA were identified between molar (1.86 ± 0.88 mm) and premolar (2.59 ± 0.53 mm) teeth in ex vivo specimens. These trends were confirmed in full-mouth cadaver imaging and in vivo human validation. Power analysis indicated 80% statistical power to detect clinically meaningful differences in STA dimensions across tooth types.ConclusionsSupracrestal tissue attachment is not uniform across the dentition and varies depending on the tooth type. High-frequency US provides a robust, noninvasive modality for direct anatomical measurement and may improve the quantitative assessment of periodontal structures in clinical practice.Advances in knowledgeThis study challenges the long-standing assumption of uniform STA and introduces a validated US-based method for direct anatomical measurement. The findings highlight clinically relevant tooth-type variation and support the integration of high-frequency US into periodontal diagnostics and treatment planning.

papers.title: Beyond breathing: Lung as a sensory organ.
papers.abstract: The lung, one the largest branching organs in our body and vital for survival at first breath, is commonly known as the gas exchange organ. Recent novel findings on lung sensing cells, molecules, and lung-brain crosstalk in the emerging discipline of interoception have highlighted the consideration of the lung as a sensory organ. Acknowledging the central importance of lung sensing to human health and disease, the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute convened a workshop to synthesize the past, current, and future of lung sensing research, with in-person presentations by approximately 20 interdisciplinary experts and a large virtual audience. Here, we highlight the key topics discussed and summarize a blueprint for the future in this important field.
